heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
KEP-2572: Defining the Kubernetes Release Cadence

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer: Kubernetes changed its release cadence from four to three releases per year (officially in April 2021; 1.22 was the first longer-cycle release). The reasons given: as the project matured, the number of enhancements per cycle kept growing, increasing the burden on contributors and the Release Engineering team, while downstream consumers and integrators struggled to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases. Three releases a year was seen as balancing stakeholder needs. Consumers and integrators get longer support terms for each minor version, since the previous three releases are supported for a longer period. Contributors get more time to mature enhancements and get them production-ready. SIG Release and Release Engineering get lower management overhead, freeing time to improve release quality and tooling. The cadence also helps the community plan upgrades and stay up to date. The KEP adds that SIG Release would have only 3 patch releases to maintain instead of up to 4 overlapping, more time for transitions between release teams, and possibly more shadows. In the community discussion, participants argued that most organizations couldn't keep up with quarterly upgrades for production clusters. Some also noted concerns about larger releases and longer alpha-to-stable latency. That discussion is lower-authority material.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer: The built-in Pod Security admission controller (Pod Security Admission, the `PodSecurity` admission plugin) enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree. It replaced the deprecated and since-removed PodSecurityPolicy. It applies restrictions at the namespace level when pods are created. Namespaces opt in through labels, and there are three modes: enforce, audit and warn. It covers the three standard policies: privileged, baseline and restricted. It is stable (GA) from v1.25 and enabled by default. You can also configure cluster-wide defaults and exemptions for usernames, runtime classes and namespaces. You do this with a PodSecurityConfiguration passed to kube-apiserver via `--admission-control-config-file`.

answer.question: Why was PodSecurityPolicy replaced instead of fixed?
answer.answer:
According to the Kubernetes v1.25 release blog, the updates needed to improve PodSecurityPolicy's usability would have introduced breaking changes. So it was removed in favor of a more user-friendly replacement, Pod Security Admission. PSP was deprecated in v1.21 and removed in v1.25. Pod Security Admission graduated to Stable in v1.25.

The PSP deprecation blog adds the thinking behind the replacement. A robust ecosystem of external admission controllers already exists, so the replacement doesn't need to be all things to all people. The main advantage of a built-in admission controller is simplicity of deployment and adoption. The replacement was therefore designed to be as simple as practically possible while still being flexible enough for production use at scale.

Pod Security Admission enforces the pod security standards at the namespace level. It makes basic pod security easier to enforce without deep security knowledge, and it can be combined with third-party solutions for more sophisticated cases.

All of these sources are tier-6 blog posts.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer: Yes, until 1.24. Before version 1.24, Kubernetes automatically generated Secret-based tokens for ServiceAccounts. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate became beta and enabled by default. With it enabled, Secret objects holding service account tokens are no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount; the Token Controller stops auto-creating them. Instead you get tokens through the TokenRequest API. If you need a non-expiring token, you create a Secret yourself and the token controller populates it. From 1.29, leftover auto-generated legacy tokens are marked invalid if unused for a period (one year by default), and are later purged by the control plane if they stay unused.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: According to KEP-2799, once BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in 1.22, Pods got their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API and had them mounted as a projected volume. The release notes show that from 1.24 the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature gate was beta and enabled by default, so Secret objects holding tokens were no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount. Users were pointed to the TokenRequest API instead, or to manually creating a Secret if they need a non-expiring token. The KEP also notes the gate was turned on as soon as it was implemented because it added no new code and helps keep new clusters in a good state.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer:
Yes. As of 1.36 (and so at 1.37), the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate is beta and enabled by default. With it enabled, the API server rejects IPv4 addresses whose octets have leading zeros (for example `010.000.000.005` instead of `10.0.0.5`). It also rejects IPv4-mapped IPv6 values and ambiguous CIDR values.

The stricter check applies only to fields in built-in API kinds. It does not apply to custom resource kinds, Kubernetes configuration files or command-line arguments.

In 1.33–1.35 the gate was alpha and off by default. In that state the API server only returns a warning that such values will be rejected in the future.

The KEP claims stable, but the observed stage at 1.37 is beta; this was already flagged and resolved in favour of the observed stage.

The 1.23 changelog said Kubernetes would keep allowing leading zeros for compatibility. That statement was valid only in 1.23 and is superseded by the current default-on stricter validation.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer: The value was accepted, not rejected. StrictIPCIDRValidation was alpha and off by default in 1.33–1.35, and became beta and on by default in 1.36. Before that, Kubernetes kept allowing leading zeros in IPv4 addresses so it would not break compatibility, even after Go 1.17's parsers began rejecting them. Kubernetes reads such octets as decimal: the legacy sloppy parsers ignore the extra zeros, so "012.000.001.002" becomes 12.0.1.2. Libc-based code may instead read them as octal (10.0.1.2), which is the ambiguity behind CVE-2021-29923. For Services in particular, the API server has returned a warning for non-standard IP values since 1.27, e.g. 'non-standard IP address "05.06.07.08" will be considered invalid in a future Kubernetes release: use "5.6.7.8"'. With the gate disabled, creating an object with such a value still succeeds but produces a warning that it will be rejected in the future.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Validation was tightened mainly for security. Kubernetes had long been too lax with IP and CIDR strings in API fields. It accepted anything Go's net.ParseIP and net.ParseCIDR accepted, even strings with ambiguous meanings that could cause security problems. Examples are IPv4 octets with leading zeros (e.g. 172.030.099.099) and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values (e.g. ::ffff:192.168.0.1). Such values are dangerous when different components read the same string as different IP addresses, as in CVE-2021-29923.

Go 1.17 changed its handling of leading-zero IPs to avoid that CVE. After that, there was consensus that Kubernetes API validation should become stricter too. It was not done right away to avoid retroactively invalidating existing API objects. KEP-4858 is the plan for finally doing it. Its goal is to make ambiguously-interpretable IPs/CIDRs impossible, at least in new clusters.

answer.question: How long does a Kubernetes minor release receive patch support?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes 1.19 and newer get roughly 14 months of patch support for each minor release series. This breaks down into two phases:

- **Standard period:** the first twelve months. This is why the docs describe it as "approximately 1 year" of patch support.
- **Maintenance mode:** a further two months. During this time Release Managers may cut extra releases only to fix CVE-assigned vulnerabilities, dependency issues (including base image updates) and critical core component issues.

After maintenance mode the series is end of life, and cherry picks to its branch are closed soon afterwards.

Kubernetes 1.18 and older received approximately 9 months of patch support. KEP-1498 (Yearly Support Period) set 1.19 as the first release to get a year of support.

heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
According to KEP-1498, the extension was made in response to an end-user request. Business cycles (financial, certification, sales, vacation, HR and others) are overwhelmingly annual, so many users want support cycles of at least a year in the projects they depend on. Nine months was described as an irregular period compared with most companies' planning, operations and financial cycles.

A survey run by WG LTS in early 2019 showed that a significant share of users did not upgrade within the 9-month window. About a third of users had production machines on versions that were out of support. The survey suggested that these users would stay on supported versions if patch support lasted 12-14 months, which would bring more than 80% of users onto supported versions instead of 50-60%. This seemed to hold whether users ran DIY builds or commercially vendored distributions. A yearly period was seen as giving users the cushion they wanted and as fitting better with familiar annual planning.

The KEP also called lengthening the window toward one year a relatively minor change that looked workable to implement. It saw this as a meaningful first response to users, and keeping the change small would let the project discover and address unknowns.

The proposal was 14 months of support: essentially 12 months of support plus a 2-month upgrade period. Kubernetes 1.19 was planned as the first release to get a year of patch support. A blog post confirms that since v1.19 the project has provided 12-14 months of patch releases, so users can adopt versions on an annual upgrade cycle.

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
Use a structured authorization configuration file rather than command-line flags. Pass its path to kube-apiserver with `--authorization-config`. Multiple webhooks, webhook failure policy and CEL pre-filter rules are only available through this file (chunk 4308). You cannot combine `--authorization-config` with `--authorization-mode` (chunk 4312).

The file is an `AuthorizationConfiguration` object (`apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1`) with an `authorizers` list. Requests are checked in the order the authorizers are listed. More than one authorizer of type `Webhook` is allowed, but at most one of each other type, such as Node or RBAC (chunks 4309, 16403).

Each `Webhook` entry has:
- a required `name`
- a `webhook` block containing:
  - `timeout` (required, at most 30s)
  - `subjectAccessReviewVersion` (required; v1 or v1beta1)
  - `matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion` (v1)
  - `failurePolicy` (required): `Deny` rejects the request; `NoOpinion` passes it on to later authorizers
  - optional `authorizedTTL` / `unauthorizedTTL` and the `cacheAuthorizedRequests` / `cacheUnauthorizedRequests` caching settings
  - `connectionInfo`, either `type: KubeConfigFile` with a `kubeConfigFile` path, or `InClusterConfig`
  - optional `matchConditions`: CEL expressions that decide whether a request is sent to that webhook (chunk 4309)

The kubeconfig file pointed to by `kubeConfigFile` uses the same format as the Webhook mode file: `clusters` is the remote service and `users` is the API server's credentials (chunks 6124, 16403).

For example, the documented config lists a `Webhook` named `webhook` (with `failurePolicy: Deny` and matchConditions), then `Node`, then `RBAC`, then a second `Webhook` named `in-cluster-authorizer` (with `failurePolicy: NoOpinion`). The API server reloads the authorizer chain automatically when the file changes (chunks 4308, 4309).

With only `--authorization-mode`, you can enable just a single webhook (chunk 16386).

answer.question: Can I write an RBAC rule that explicitly denies a permission?
answer.answer: No. RBAC permissions are purely additive: a Role or ClusterRole contains rules that grant a set of permissions, and there are no "deny" rules. The Authorization docs say the same thing, noting that Kubernetes RBAC does not provide negative (deny) access rules. One consequence is that `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC` has the same effect as `AlwaysAllow` alone. When RBAC does not allow a request, it does not issue an explicit deny; the next authorizer in the configured chain is consulted. For example, with `RBAC,ABAC`, a request allowed by either policy is allowed. You can only restrict access by granting narrowly, for example with specific resources, verbs and resourceNames, and by following least privilege.

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
As of 1.37, kube-proxy's `ipvs` mode still works on Linux nodes, but it has been deprecated since v1.35. kube-proxy prints a warning when started in `ipvs` mode, and in 1.37 kubeadm also added a warning about the deprecation.

The planned timeline:
- **v1.40:** `ipvs` support will be disabled by default. You can re-enable it with the `KubeProxyIPVS` feature gate. Without that override, kube-proxy will exit with an error listing the valid modes (`iptables` and `nftables`).
- **v1.43:** `ipvs` mode will be fully removed from the tree, and it will not be maintained anywhere else.

The recommended replacement is the `nftables` proxy mode, which became GA in 1.33. It is described as essentially a replacement for both `iptables` and `ipvs`, with better performance than either. If your Linux nodes run kernels too old for `nftables`, use `iptables` mode instead; it is still the default, and its performance has improved greatly since `ipvs` was introduced. The kernels too old for `nftables` are expected to be out of LTS by the end of 2026.

answer.question: Should a new controller watch Endpoints or EndpointSlices to find a Service's backends?
answer.answer:
A new controller should watch EndpointSlices. The Endpoints API has been deprecated since v1.33, and the docs recommend that all clients use the EndpointSlice API instead. The docs give three reasons:
- Endpoints does not support dual-stack clusters.
- It lacks the information needed for newer features such as trafficDistribution.
- It truncates the endpoint list when it is too long to fit in a single object (the limit is 1000 endpoints).

KEP-4974 adds that kube-proxy no longer uses Endpoints at all. It also aims for a world where clusters run with the Endpoints and EndpointSlice mirroring controllers disabled, so Endpoints objects may not even be generated. Even user-written Endpoints for selectorless Services should be replaced by EndpointSlices created directly.

One practical difference to handle: a Service has exactly one Endpoints object, but it can have many EndpointSlices. You get more than one slice per IP family in dual-stack, per port set during rollouts, or when there are more than about 100 endpoints. Your controller should therefore select slices by the `kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>` label and aggregate across them.

The evidence also contains a minor disagreement about mirroring, which does not affect this recommendation. The docs say Endpoints are mirrored unless the skip-mirror label is "true"; a KEP-752 test-plan line says the opposite. The tier-1 docs wording is taken as correct.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 dual-stack was off by default, and you had to turn it on yourself. To do that, you enabled the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant components and set dual-stack (IPv4,IPv6) network assignments:
- kube-apiserver: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`
- kube-controller-manager: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. The node CIDR mask sizes (`--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4|--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6`) default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6.
- kubelet: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`
- kube-proxy: `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`

Prerequisites were Kubernetes 1.20 or later, provider support for routable IPv4/IPv6 node interfaces, and a network plugin that supports dual-stack (such as Kubenet or Calico). In 1.20 the feature had been reimplemented to support dual-stack Services and was still alpha. Only from 1.21 did it become beta and enabled by default.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how could a Service prefer endpoints on the same node as the client?
answer.answer:
In Kubernetes 1.20 this was done with Service Topology, an alpha feature (since v1.17). With Service Topology enabled in the cluster, you set the `topologyKeys` field on the Service spec. It is a preference-ordered list of Node labels used to sort endpoints.

Traffic goes to a Node whose value for the first label matches the client Node's value. If there is no backend on a matching Node, the next label is tried, and so on. If no label matches, traffic is rejected, as if the Service had no backends. The special value `"*"` means "any topology" and only makes sense as the last entry.

To prefer node-local endpoints but fall back to any endpoint in the cluster, use:

```yaml
topologyKeys:
  - "kubernetes.io/hostname"
  - "*"
```

Using only `["kubernetes.io/hostname"]` sends traffic solely to endpoints on the same node, and fails if none exist there. You can also chain hostname, then `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, then `topology.kubernetes.io/region`, optionally ending with `"*"`. If `topologyKeys` is empty or not set, no topology constraints apply.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
kube-proxy's nftables mode became generally available (GA) in Kubernetes v1.33. Even after GA, iptables stayed the default mode. You opt into nftables with `--proxy-mode nftables` or with `mode: nftables` in the config file.

The path to GA was:
- **v1.29 (alpha):** an nftables backend was added to kube-proxy. The default Linux implementation was iptables, and nftables was presented as its successor that addresses iptables' performance problems.
- **v1.31 (beta):** the mode moved to beta behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which became enabled by default. At that stage it required Linux kernel 5.13 or later. It might not be compatible with all network plugins, and some NodePort behaviour differed from iptables mode.
- **v1.33 (GA):** the KEP's GA criteria included at least two releases since beta, non-trivial real-world usage, and no blocking bugs. The KEP is observed as stable.

Later developments:
- **v1.35:** ipvs mode was deprecated, and nftables was named the recommended replacement on Linux.
- **v1.37:** kubeadm explicitly sets the mode to iptables when it is unset. kube-proxy warns if the mode isn't explicitly set, as part of a planned future transition to nftables as the default. The 1.37 changelog also repeats that nftables became GA in v1.33.

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDRs (feature gate MultiCIDRServiceAllocator, tracked as KEP-1880 by SIG Network) went through three stages:

- **Alpha, v1.27–v1.30:** the gate was off by default.
- **Beta, v1.31–v1.32:** still off by default. To use the feature you had to enable the gate and the networking v1beta1 API group; it lets you reconfigure Service CIDR ranges dynamically. Also in 1.31, users of the feature got a dual-write strategy on the new ClusterIP allocators by default. You could opt out by enabling the DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate.
- **Stable (GA), v1.33:** the gate defaults to true and is locked. The 1.33 changelog marks this as action required: administrators and distributions can define the cluster Service CIDR through the ServiceCIDR API object. They can use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to restrict new ranges or to keep only one ServiceCIDR per cluster. DisableAllocatorDualWrite moved to beta (off by default) in the same release.

The older 1.24–1.26 KEP draft disagrees on timing. Its example assumes the alpha gate arrives in 1.25, but the feature-gate reference shows alpha only from 1.27. The observed stages take precedence over the draft's claim.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
Per KEP-3866 and the v1.29 release blog, the default kube-proxy implementation on Linux was based on iptables, but problems with iptables led to the development of nftables as its successor. Development on iptables has mostly stopped, and new features and performance improvements go mainly into nftables. The blog also notes that some Linux distributions had started to deprecate and remove iptables, and that nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. The KEP's drawbacks section warns that doing nothing would eventually leave many users unable to use the default proxy implementation.

The KEP gives further motivations:
- SIG Network supports both the iptables and ipvs backends and feels it cannot drop ipvs because of perceived iptables performance problems. A backend as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as performant as ipvs could eventually let both be deprecated, leaving only one Linux backend to support.
- Writing a new backend would force a review of the poorly designed shared "core kube-proxy" code, helping the cleanup and refactoring needed for a reusable kube-proxy library (KEP-3786).
- None of the existing nftables-based implementations (kube-nftlb, nfproxy, kpng's nft backend) was suitable to adopt directly or to use as a starting point.

A later blog post adds that nftables allows incremental updates sized only to what changed, and private per-component tables that avoid the global lock contention seen with iptables. This makes kube-proxy updates far more efficient than with iptables.
